topic.subject: science
topic.title: Electricity
topic.scope: charge, current, potential difference, Ohm's law, resistance and resistivity, series and parallel, heating effect, power

nodes.name: Current is rate of flow of charge
Electrons flow from negative to positive
Potential difference is work per unit charge
V is directly proportional to I
Resistance depends on length and area
Power is rate of energy consumption

misconceptions.statement: The current coming out of a bulb is less than the current going into it.
misconceptions.why: Students think of electricity as a fuel that is consumed to produce light.
misconceptions.fix: Current is the flow of charges, and charges are not consumed; they circulate. The same number of electrons enters and leaves the bulb every second.

probe.question: In a simple circuit with one bulb, how does the current at the positive terminal compare to the negative terminal?
probe.wrong_answer: It is less at the negative terminal because the bulb used some up.

misconceptions.root_belief: a resource is used up during a process

misconceptions.statement: A battery always supplies the same amount of current regardless of what is connected to it.
misconceptions.why: They confuse the fixed voltage rating of a battery with a fixed current output.
misconceptions.fix: A battery maintains a constant potential difference, but the current it supplies depends on the total resistance of the circuit (I = V/R).

probe.question: If I replace a 5 ohm bulb with a 10 ohm bulb in a circuit with a 9V battery, what happens to the current from the battery?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays the same because the battery is the same.

misconceptions.root_belief: a source provides a constant amount of effect

misconceptions.statement: Resistance of a conductor changes when the applied voltage changes.
misconceptions.why: They interpret the mathematical formula R = V/I as a causal relationship where V and I determine R.
misconceptions.fix: For an ohmic conductor, resistance is a constant property; changing V causes a proportional change in I, keeping the ratio R constant.

probe.question: If the voltage across a resistor is doubled, what happens to its resistance?

misconceptions.root_belief: mathematical variables always imply physical causation

misconceptions.statement: If you cut a wire in half, its resistivity also becomes half.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse resistance (an extrinsic property) with resistivity (an intrinsic property).
misconceptions.fix: Resistivity is a characteristic property of the material and does not change with the dimensions of the object.

probe.question: A copper wire of length L is stretched to 2L. What happens to its resistivity?
probe.wrong_answer: It doubles because there is more length.

misconceptions.root_belief: properties of a part match the whole

misconceptions.statement: In a series circuit, the bulb closer to the positive terminal glows brighter because it gets the current first.
misconceptions.why: They view electricity as a sequential flow that loses 'strength' as it hits obstacles.
misconceptions.fix: In a series circuit, the current is identical at every point because charge cannot accumulate anywhere.

probe.question: Two identical bulbs are in series. Which one is brighter?
probe.wrong_answer: The one closer to the battery.

misconceptions.root_belief: sequential flow loses energy over distance

misconceptions.statement: Adding more resistors in parallel increases the total resistance of the circuit.
misconceptions.why: They overgeneralize the rule for series circuits where adding more components increases resistance.
misconceptions.fix: Adding a parallel path provides more routes for current to flow, which reduces total resistance.

probe.question: If you add a 1000 ohm resistor in parallel to a 1 ohm resistor, what happens to total resistance?
probe.wrong_answer: It increases because 1000 is a large number.

misconceptions.root_belief: adding more of something increases the total

misconceptions.statement: Conventional current flows from positive to negative because that is the direction electrons move.
misconceptions.why: They assume 'current' and 'electron flow' are the same thing and that 'positive' is the natural starting point.
misconceptions.fix: Electrons are negatively charged and flow from the negative terminal to the positive terminal; conventional current is in the opposite direction.

probe.question: In which direction do electrons move in a circuit?

misconceptions.statement: If there is no current flowing in a wire, the potential difference across its ends must be zero.
misconceptions.why: They believe potential difference is a result of flow rather than the cause of it.
misconceptions.fix: A battery has a potential difference across its terminals even when it is not connected to a circuit.

probe.question: A battery is sitting on a table not connected to anything. Is there a potential difference between its terminals?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because no current is flowing.

misconceptions.root_belief: no observable effect means no cause exists

misconceptions.statement: A wire with very low resistance will not get hot even if a very high current flows through it.
misconceptions.why: They focus only on the 'R' in Joule's Law and ignore the 'I squared' term.
misconceptions.fix: Heat depends on both current and resistance; a low resistance wire can get very hot if the current is high enough.

probe.question: Why does a short circuit cause a fire if the wires have low resistance?
probe.wrong_answer: The resistance must have suddenly increased.

misconceptions.root_belief: only one factor determines the outcome

misconceptions.statement: In a parallel circuit, the total voltage of the battery is divided among the different branches.
misconceptions.why: They confuse the voltage rule for series circuits with the rule for parallel circuits.
misconceptions.fix: In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across each branch is equal to the potential difference across the source.

probe.question: Three 1.5V bulbs are connected in parallel to a 1.5V cell. What is the voltage across each bulb?

misconceptions.statement: When you turn on a switch, electrons travel from the battery to the bulb to make it light up.
misconceptions.why: They use a water-pipe analogy where the pipe starts empty and must be filled.
misconceptions.fix: The wire is already full of electrons; the battery provides the push that makes all electrons start moving almost instantaneously.

probe.question: Why does a bulb light up immediately when the switch is far away?
probe.wrong_answer: Electrons travel at the speed of light.

misconceptions.root_belief: motion requires a travel time from source

misconceptions.statement: Only insulators have resistance; perfect conductors like copper have zero resistance.
misconceptions.why: They associate 'resistance' with 'stopping' and think 'conductors' don't stop anything.
misconceptions.fix: All materials except superconductors offer some resistance to the flow of current due to internal collisions.

probe.question: Does a standard copper connecting wire have any resistance?
